xu.summary: The preface explains why Tao Yuanming took the post of magistrate of Pengze and then gave it up. His family was poor and he sought office, but his nature was simple and natural, he could not bend his heart to deal with officialdom, and when his sister died he resigned and wrote this piece.
xu.translation:
My family was poor, and farming did not provide enough to support us. The house was full of young children, the jars had no grain stored, and I saw no way to earn our living. Relatives and old friends mostly urged me to take a post as an official, and I felt a stir of wish for it, but found no road. Then there was business in the four quarters, and the lords took kindness and love as a virtue; my uncle, because I was poor and hard-pressed, got me a post in a small town. At that time the wind and waves had not settled, and I feared service far away. Pengze was a hundred li from home, and the profit of its official fields was enough to make wine, so I asked for it.
After only a few days, I felt a longing to go home. Why? My nature is natural, and cannot be got by forcing and driving. Hunger and cold may be sharp, but going against myself hurts me more. In my past dealings with officials I was always working like a servant for my mouth and belly. Then I felt a sad heaviness and deep shame at the aim of my whole life. I still hoped to wait for one harvest, and then gather up my robe and slip away by night.
Soon after, my sister, Madam Cheng, died at Wuchang, and my heart was set on hurrying to her funeral, so I removed myself from my post. From midautumn to winter I was in office a little over eighty days. As events went with my heart, I named this piece 'Going Home'. It was the eleventh month of the year yisi.

glossary.note: A variant of the character for 'bottle', a pottery vessel. The phrase means there was no grain stored in the house.
A local official of fairly high rank; here it loosely means a post such as county magistrate.
A county, in the area of today's Hukou in Jiangxi. Tao Yuanming served as its magistrate.
Fields set aside in ancient times to pay an official, whose income went to the man in the post.
To strain, to act unnaturally, to restrain oneself against one's own nature.
One year's crop; ren means grain ripening.
To hurry quickly, here to hurry to a funeral.

glossary.en: yi si sui - the year yisi
glossary.note: The first year of Yixi under Emperor An of Jin, which is 405.

xu.background: In 405, the first year of Yixi, Tao Yuanming became magistrate of Pengze, and after a little over eighty days in office he resigned and went back to the land, never to take office again. This preface explains how it came about.

ci.summary: This is the piece of feeling Tao Yuanming wrote after resigning and returning home. In turn it describes the joy of the journey back, the pleasures of the fields and garden at home, his decision to withdraw from the world, and the attitude of accepting what Heaven gives and being content with it. The feeling is sincere and the language plain and natural.
ci.translation:
Let me go home! The fields and garden are going to weeds - why not return? I made my own heart the slave of my body; why should I brood and grieve alone? I see that what is past cannot be mended, and know that what is to come can still be followed. I have indeed wandered off the road, but not far; I sense that today is right and yesterday was wrong.
The boat sways far and lightly rises; the wind blows soft and stirs my robe. I ask a traveller about the road ahead, and resent that the morning light is so faint. Then I catch sight of my roof, and in joy I run. The servants welcome me; my young children wait at the gate. The three paths are going to ruin, but the pine and chrysanthemum still stand. I lead the little ones into the house; there is wine filling the jar. I draw a pot and cup to pour myself a drink, and glance at the garden branches to cheer my face. Leaning at the south window, I let my pride roam, and I see how easily a room just big enough for the knees gives peace. In the garden I walk each day and it grows into a pleasure; the gate is set but always shut. I take my staff to help my age and rest as I go, from time to time lifting my head to gaze far off. The clouds, with no purpose, come out of the mountain peaks; the birds, tired of flying, know to return. The light dims and is about to enter the dark; I stroke a lone pine and linger.
Let me go home! I ask to end my dealings and cut off my wanderings. The world and I have gone different ways; if I drive out again, what would I look for? I take pleasure in the friendly talk of kin, and enjoy zither and books to dispel care. The farmers tell me that spring has come, and there will be work in the western fields. Some order a covered cart; some pole a lone boat. I follow a winding hollow into a valley, and also go up and down over rough hills. The trees flourish and lean towards bloom, and the springs begin to trickle. I am glad that all things have their season, and feel that my own life is drawing to its close.
It is over! How much longer shall I lodge in this body between heaven and earth? Why not leave my heart free to go or stay? Why rush about in such hurry - where do I wish to go? Wealth and rank are not what I want; the realm of the Lord of Heaven cannot be hoped for. Thinking of a fine day, I go out alone; sometimes I plant my staff and weed and earth up the crops. I climb the eastern bank and whistle at leisure; I stand by a clear stream and make a poem. I will simply ride the changes until I come to my end, and take joy in Heaven's decree - what is there to doubt?

keyLines.line: 既自以心為形役，奚惆悵而獨悲
keyLines.en: I made my own heart the slave of my body; why should I brood and grieve alone?
keyLines.note: He blames himself for letting his spirit be driven by his body and by pay; this is the root reason for resigning.

keyLines.line: 悟已往之不諫，知來者之可追
keyLines.en: I see that what is past cannot be mended, and know that what is to come can still be followed.
keyLines.note: What has gone cannot be recalled, but the future can still be set right.

keyLines.line: 雲無心以出岫，鳥倦飛而知還
keyLines.en: The clouds, with no purpose, come out of the mountain peaks; the birds, tired of flying, know to return.
keyLines.note: Clouds and birds stand for himself, who has at last come back to nature. It is the best-known scene in the whole piece.

keyLines.en: I will simply ride the changes until I come to my end, and take joy in Heaven's decree - what is there to doubt?
keyLines.note: The closing line expresses a calm acceptance of what Heaven decides.

glossary.en: xing yi - slave of the body
glossary.note: The spirit driven by the body, or by fame and profit.
The first light, when the daylight is still dim.
A simple dwelling; heng is a crossbar that serves as the gate.
Jiang Xu of the Han made three paths in his courtyard; later it meant a recluse's garden.

glossary.en: rong xi - room for the knees
glossary.note: A hut just big enough to hold one's knees, meaning a very small dwelling.
About to finish; it refers to life coming near its end.

glossary.en: di xiang - the Lord of Heaven's country
glossary.note: The place where the Lord of Heaven lives, meaning to become an immortal.

ci.background: In 405 Tao Yuanming resigned as magistrate of Pengze and went back to live in the countryside. Legend says he refused to bow to a visiting inspector for the sake of five pecks of rice, and so hung up his cap and left. This ci is his first declaration after retiring, and later readers rank it as a masterpiece of the rhapsody and ci forms of the Wei and Jin periods.
